abstract.para: This section describes how to measure operating system latencies using the cyclictest tool. It guides you through installing the test suite on &suselinux; 16.1. It also details running the benchmark to generate latency histogram files.

topic.para: The cyclictest command is part of the real-time kernel test suite, contained in the rt-tests RPM package distributed as part of &suselinux; 16.1.
Before you run this test, make sure your hardware is configured as described in , and that you are logged in as &rootuser; or can run commands with sudo.

Start cyclictest. For example, to run 1000 cycles with a latency histogram tracked up to 1000 microseconds, execute:
By default, cyclictest writes the histogram data to standard output after the run. To save it to a file for later analysis instead, redirect the output:
Analyze the recorded minimal, actual, average and maximum latencies.
A typical result on a multi-core system looks like:
step.screen:
cyclictest --loops=1000 --histogram=1000 policy: fifo: loadavg: 0.12 0.08 0.03 1/342 4821
T: 0 ( 4822) P:99 I:1000 C: 1000 Min: 4 Act: 6 Avg: 7 Max: 31 T: 1 ( 4823) P:99 I:1500 C: 667 Min: 3 Act: 5 Avg: 6 Max: 24
step.para: Each line reports one measurement thread (T:), its process ID, scheduling priority (P:) and interval in microseconds (I:). Four values matter for evaluation: Min, Act (the latency of the most recent cycle), Avg and Max. All four are reported in microseconds by default. Use --nsec if you need nanosecond resolution.

Max is the value to compare against the deadline of your application: it is the single worst-case scheduling latency observed during the run. As a rough order of magnitude, well-tuned real-time systems generally report Max values in the tens of microseconds. Results climbing into the hundreds of microseconds suggest an unresolved source of interference, and results in the thousands of microseconds indicate the system is not meeting real-time deadlines at all. These figures vary by hardware, workload and kernel configuration. Compare this Max value against the Max Latency reported by hwlatdetect in . Per , cyclictest is expected to report somewhat higher latencies, since it includes scheduling and interrupt handling overhead that hwlatdetect does not measure.

The Max value from cyclictest includes hardware latency plus kernel scheduling overhead. The Max Latency value from hwlatdetect does not. So cyclictest is expected to report a higher number. The two tools are not measuring the same thing.
What matters is the size of the gap. A small gap is normal software overhead. A gap of orders of magnitude points to a real problem in the operating system, not the hardware.
